description: The compaction-to-read-latency causal chain, laid out top to bottom: backlog, SSTable count, SSTables per read, disk held by obsolete files, growth against headroom, and the read latency that results.

options.content:
This dashboard answers one question: **why do reads get worse over hours?**

It is laid out as a causal chain, and it reads **down the page**. Compaction falls behind, so live
SSTable count rises, so SSTables touched per read rises, so read latency climbs. Start at the top
and stop at the first section that looks wrong; everything below it is a consequence.

1. **Compaction falls behind.** Backlog rising while completion rate stays flat is the failure.
   A backlog that spikes and drains is normal.
2. **Compaction in flight.** How far the current compactions have got, and how many bytes are left.
3. **SSTable count rises.** The first visible consequence of a backlog.
4. **SSTables per read rises.** The mechanism. A read that must merge more SSTables costs more.
5. **Space held by obsolete SSTables.** A live/total ratio well under 1 means disk is occupied by
   files that compaction has superseded but not yet dropped.
6. **Storage growth and headroom.** Growth rate, and how long the data filesystem lasts at it.
7. **Filesystem.** Used and free per mount, so the projection above can be sanity-checked.
8. **Outcome.** Read latency: the thing all of the above explains.

**Label trap.** Two families name the same concepts differently, and it is upstream's naming, not a
bug here. `cassandra_compaction_progress_*` carries **`cassandra_keyspace`** and
**`cassandra_table`**; every other per-table family (`cassandra_table_*`) carries bare **`keyspace`**
and **`table`**. Both are in the Group by dropdown. A panel using one will collapse to a single
series if you pick the other, and joining across the two families requires matching on different
label names.

**Empty per-table panels are filtered, not broken.** The per-table panels use `topk` over series
with a non-zero value, so idle system tables do not crowd out the tables under test.

panels.description: Pending compaction tasks per node (left axis, `cassandra_compaction_tasks_pending`) against compactions finished per second (right axis, rate of `cassandra_compaction_tasks_completed_total`). The failure mode is backlog climbing while completion stays flat: compaction is running as fast as it can and still losing. Backlog climbing WITH completion means the write rate simply exceeds compaction throughput.
panels.title: Compaction backlog vs completion rate

panels.description: `cassandra_table_compaction_pending`, restricted to tables with a non-zero backlog and cut to the ten largest. This is where a node-level backlog actually lives. Labels: bare `keyspace` and `table`.
panels.title: Pending compactions by table (top 10)

panels.description: `cassandra_compaction_progress_completed_bytes` divided by `cassandra_compaction_progress_size_bytes` for each compaction currently running. A line that climbs to 1 and disappears is a compaction finishing. A line that barely moves is a long compaction holding a slot. Labels on this family are PREFIXED: `cassandra_keyspace` and `cassandra_table`, not the bare names used elsewhere.
panels.title: Compaction progress (completed / total)

panels.description: Total size minus completed bytes for each running compaction. Read with the panel on the left: a high fraction complete on a very large compaction can still be hours of work.
panels.title: Compaction bytes remaining

panels.description: `cassandra_table_sstable_count_live`, non-zero series only, ten largest. This is the first visible consequence of section 1. A count that ratchets up and never comes down is a compaction backlog you can see. Labels: bare `keyspace` and `table`.
panels.title: Live SSTable count by table (top 10)

panels.description: The same metric aggregated by the Group by dimension. Honours host_name, cassandra_build, cluster, and the bare `keyspace` and `table`. It does NOT carry `cassandra_keyspace` or `cassandra_table`: choosing either of those collapses this panel to one series.
panels.title: Live SSTable count by $groupby

panels.description: The mechanism that turns SSTable count into latency. Shown as a ladder rather than through the Percentile variable on purpose: this family publishes only p50, p99 and max, so a Percentile of p999 would return nothing. p99 pulling away from p50 means a minority of reads is merging many more files.
panels.title: SSTables per read — p50, p99 and max together

panels.description: The same p99, left per node so a single lagging node is visible. Non-zero series only, ten largest.
panels.title: SSTables per read p99 by table and node (top 10)

panels.description: `cassandra_table_disk_space_live_bytes` over `cassandra_table_disk_space_total_bytes`. Live counts only SSTables a read can reach; total counts everything on disk for the table. A ratio well under 1 is space held by superseded files that have not been dropped yet. Shown as the ten LOWEST ratios, because low is the interesting end. Tables with no data on disk are excluded by the non-zero denominator.
panels.title: Live / total disk ratio by table (bottom 10)

panels.description: `cassandra_table_disk_space_total_bytes`, ten largest. The absolute companion to the ratio on the left: a poor ratio on a tiny table costs nothing.
panels.title: Table disk space, total on disk (top 10)

panels.description: `cassandra_storage_load_bytes`, the total the node reports for its own data. Diverging lines across nodes mean an uneven token range or a node that is not compacting.
panels.title: Storage load per node

panels.description: `deriv()` of storage load over a 15 minute window, in bytes per second. Negative means compaction is reclaiming faster than writes arrive. The 15 minute window is deliberately wider than the scrape interval so a single compaction release does not dominate.
panels.title: Storage growth rate

panels.description: Free bytes on the largest filesystem for the node, divided by the current storage growth rate. The largest filesystem is the data mount on any normal layout; narrow Mount point if it is not. Growth at or below zero is clamped to 1 byte per second, so a flat or shrinking dataset shows an absurdly large time rather than an error. This is a straight-line projection from the last 15 minutes, not a forecast.

targets.expr: max by (host_name) (system_filesystem_usage_bytes{state="free", host_name=~"$host", mountpoint=~"$mountpoint"}) / clamp_min(max by (host_name) (deriv(cassandra_storage_load_bytes{host_name=~"$host"}[15m])), 1)

panels.title: Projected time until the data filesystem is full

panels.description: Used bytes as a percentage of used plus free plus reserved, kept per mount so the data mount is never averaged with the root partition. With Mount point on All this includes boot partitions, which are small and static.

targets.expr: 100 * sum by (host_name, mountpoint) (system_filesystem_usage_bytes{state="used", host_name=~"$host", mountpoint=~"$mountpoint"}) / sum by (host_name, mountpoint) (system_filesystem_usage_bytes{host_name=~"$host", mountpoint=~"$mountpoint"})

panels.title: Filesystem used, per mount

panels.description: The absolute headroom behind the projection in section 6. Read this before trusting the time-to-full number.
panels.title: Filesystem free bytes, per mount
8. Outcome — the read latency all of the above explains

panels.description: `cassandra_client_request_latency_${percentile}_microseconds` for reads, divided by the Latency unit divisor. This is the symptom the whole page explains. If it climbs while sections 1 to 4 are flat, compaction is not the cause and this dashboard has answered no.
panels.title: Read latency ${percentile} per node (${latency_unit:text})

panels.description: The same gauge aggregated by the Group by dimension. The client-request family carries host_name, cluster, cassandra_build and cassandra_operation only; any keyspace or table choice collapses this panel to one series.
panels.title: Read latency ${percentile} by $groupby

panels.description: Streaming moves SSTable data between nodes. Every panel in this row is flat at zero unless a repair, a bootstrap, a decommission or a rebuild is actually running. That is the normal state of a healthy idle cluster; it is not a broken panel and not a missing metric.
panels.title: 9. Streaming and repair

panels.description: Stream sessions in flight on each node. Read it as: non-zero means this node is sending or receiving SSTable data right now, for a repair, a bootstrap, a decommission or a rebuild, and the compaction and disk panels above should be read in that light. Flat at zero is the normal state of an idle cluster and is not a broken panel.
panels.title: Active streams per node

panels.description: Bytes per second streamed into and out of each node, over all stream types. Read it as the disk and network cost the streaming operation is imposing while it runs, and compare it with the filesystem and compaction panels above: incoming stream bytes land as new SSTables and feed straight back into the compaction backlog. Flat at zero is normal unless a repair, bootstrap, decommission or rebuild is running, and is not a broken panel.
panels.title: Streaming bytes in and out

panels.description: Bytes per second streamed out of each node specifically for repair. Read it against the total outgoing rate in the panel above: the difference is bootstrap, decommission or rebuild traffic. Cassandra publishes the repair breakdown for the outgoing direction only, so there is no matching incoming series to compare against. Flat at zero is normal unless a repair is running and is not a broken panel.
panels.title: Repair streaming bytes out

panels.description: SSTables per second sent by each node as part of repair. Read it with the repair byte rate to its left: dividing one by the other gives the average size of the SSTables repair is moving, and many small files cost far more in compaction afterwards than the byte count suggests. Flat at zero is normal unless a repair is running and is not a broken panel.
panels.title: Repair SSTables streamed

panels.description: Rate at which each node retries a repair message. Read it as: sustained non-zero while a repair runs means the repair is struggling against a slow or flapping peer, or against internode timeouts, and the repair will take far longer than the byte rate suggests. Flat at zero is normal both when no repair is running and when a repair is running cleanly; it is not a broken panel.
panels.title: Repair retries
Compaction throughput vs JVM allocation rate
panels.description: The relationship. Left axis: bytes fed to compaction per second per node (rate of cassandra_compaction_bytes_compacted_total). Right axis: whole-JVM allocation per second per node (rate of jvm_memory_allocation_bytes_sum). The two rise together — allocation tracks compaction. Under the identical workload the difference between the allocation lines is the compaction strategy: a cursor-compaction node allocates less for the same bytes compacted. Whole-JVM allocation includes read/flush/messaging, so read it as the trend, not an exact compaction-only figure; the clean compaction-only number lives in Pyroscope.

panels.title: Allocation per byte compacted (this range)
panels.description: The verdict, normalized for work done. Bytes the JVM allocated divided by bytes compacted, over the dashboard range, per node. Dividing by compaction work cancels the fact that nodes compact different amounts, so the bars are directly comparable. A lower bar is a cheaper compaction path. min is pinned to 0 so bar length is proportional to the true value, not the min-max spread. Reads near-infinite until compaction has run enough to make the denominator non-zero. Whole-JVM allocation, comparable across nodes only under an identical workload.

list.description: Which read-latency gauge section 8 reads. The percentile is part of the metric name. The SSTables-per-read family publishes only p50, p99 and max, so section 4 shows its own ladder instead of following this variable.
list.label: Percentile
list.name: percentile

list.description: Display unit for latency. Both sides are normalised to microseconds first, so the value is the divisor: milliseconds divides by 1000, microseconds divides by 1.
list.label: Latency unit
list.name: latency_unit

list.description: Database nodes. Derived from a Cassandra-only metric, so All expands to the database nodes and never widens a panel to the load generator or the control node.
list.label: Host
list.name: host

list.description: Filesystems to show. All includes the root and boot partitions as well as the data mount. The headroom panel takes the largest filesystem per node, which is the data mount on any normal layout; narrow this variable if it is not.
list.label: Mount point
list.name: mountpoint

list.description: Dimension for the panels that say so in their title. Not every metric carries every label; a label the metric does not carry collapses that panel to one unlabelled series. Each panel names the label families it honours.
list.label: Group by
list.name: groupby

title: Compaction and Storage
